summary: Updates RFC 2132 to reclassify DHCPv4 option codes 128 to 223 as publicly defined options managed by IANA under RFC 2939. IANA is directed to make these codes available for future assignment as public DHCP options.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3942 frees up room in the DHCP option registry. A DHCP option is a numbered field that a server sends to a client to configure it, and the numbers are split between those the IETF defines and those a single site may use for itself. The second group was large and almost empty, so the memo moves most of it into the first group and gives vendors a few months to claim the codes they already use.

questions: what dhcp option codes were reclassified
how many site specific dhcp options remain
how did vendors claim reclassified dhcp options
why was dhcpv4 option space running out
subtitle: How DHCPv4 gained room for more public option codes by taking them from the little-used site-specific range.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 has 256 option codes, and the range reserved for options the IETF defines was almost used up. The alternative range, for options a single site defines for itself, was large and barely used.
tldr.mechanism: This memo reclassifies option codes 128 to 223 as publicly defined options, administered by IANA under the procedures of RFC 2939. Vendors who had already used codes in that range get six months to say so and eighteen months to write down what they used them for, after which the codes are free for new assignments.
tldr.outcome: The publicly defined range grows from 1 to 127 to 1 to 223, leaving 31 site-specific codes. Sites that were using codes in the reclassified range are told to renumber, and a site needing more than 31 must switch to suboptions. The memo changes no protocol behaviour and has no security effect of its own.

today: RFC 3942 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level. It updates RFC 2132 by moving the DHCPv4 option codes 128 to 223 from the site-specific range to the publicly defined range, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why the Option Space Ran Out
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 publicly defined options range, options 1 to 127, is nearly used up. Efforts such as RFC 3679 help extend the life of this space, because several allocated but unused option codes have been reclaimed, but ultimately the space will be exhausted. A review could be made from time to time to determine whether there are other option codes that can be reclaimed.

This document reclassifies much of the site-specific option range, which has not been widely used for its original intended purpose, to extend the publicly defined options space.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers that the IETF uses for DHCP options are running out, and one way to get more is to take them from the range that sites were supposed to use for themselves, which nobody had much use for.

sections.title: The Two Ranges of the Option Space
sections.content:
The DHCP option space, 0 to 255, is divided into two ranges. Options 1 to 127 are publicly defined options, now allocated in accordance with RFC 2939, and options 128 to 254 are site-specific options. Options 0, the pad option, and 255, the end option, are special and defined in RFC 2131.

The site-specific option range is rather large, 127 options in all, and little used. The original intent of that range was to support local, that is site-specific, configuration options, and it is difficult to believe a site would need 127 options for that purpose. Further, many DHCP client implementations do not provide a well documented means to request site-specific options from a server, or to allow applications to extract the returned option values.

Some vendors have made use of site-specific option codes that violate the intent of the range, because the options are used to configure features of their own products and are therefore specific to many sites. This usage could potentially cause problems if a site that has been using the same site-specific option codes for other purposes deploys products from one of those vendors, or if two vendors pick the same site-specific options.
sections.plainLanguage: The option codes are split in two: numbers the IETF hands out, and numbers a site may use for itself. The second group is 127 codes long and barely used, and the vendors who did use it used it in a way that was not really local, which is what causes collisions.

sections.title: The Alternatives That Were Considered
sections.content:
A longer-term solution to the eventual exhaustion of the publicly defined options space is desired, and the DHCP working group evaluated several solutions.

The first was to use options 126 and 127 to carry 16-bit options, as originally proposed by Ralph Droms in late 1996. This significantly penalizes the first option assigned to the new space, because it requires implementing 16-bit option support. Because of this, options 126 and 127 have been reclaimed under RFC 3679.

The second was to use a new magic cookie and a 16-bit option code format. This proposal penalizes the first option assigned to the new space, because it requires significant changes to clients, servers and relay agents. It could adversely impact existing clients, servers and relay agents that fail to properly check the magic cookie value. It requires support of both message formats for the foreseeable future, and it requires clients to send multiple DHCPDISCOVER messages, one for each magic cookie.

The third, and the one this document takes, is to reclassify a portion of the site-specific option codes as publicly defined. The impact is minimal, because only those sites presently using options in the reclassified range need to renumber their options.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways of making room were considered. Two of them, wider option codes and a new message format, would have made the first new option awkward to use and would have affected existing software. Reusing part of the site range was the cheapest, because only the sites already using those codes are affected.

sections.title: The Reclassification Procedure
sections.content:
The site-specific option codes 128 to 223 are reclassified as publicly defined options, which leaves 31 site-specific options, 224 to 254.

To allow the vendors that have made use of site-specific options within the reclassified range to publish their option usage and to request an official assignment of the option number to that usage, a four-step procedure is used.

First, the reclassified options, 128 to 223, are placed in the Unavailable state by IANA. They are not yet available for assignment to publicly defined options.

Second, vendors that currently use one or more of the reclassified options have six months following the publication date of the memo to notify the DHCP working group and IANA that they are using particular option numbers and to agree to document that usage in an RFC. IANA moves these options from Unavailable to Tentatively Assigned. Vendors have 18 months from the publication date to start the documentation process by submitting an Internet-Draft. The memo adds a note: if multiple vendors of an option number come forward and can demonstrate that their usage is in reasonably wide use, none of the vendors will be allowed to keep the current option number, and they must go through the normal process of getting a publicly assigned option under RFC 2939.

Third, any options still classified as Unavailable six months after the publication date are moved by IANA to the Unassigned state, and may then be assigned to any new publicly defined options in accordance with RFC 2939.

Fourth, for those options in the Tentatively Assigned state, vendors have 18 months following the publication date to submit an Internet-Draft documenting the option, and the documented usage must be consistent with the existing usage. When the option usage is published as an RFC, IANA moves the option to the Assigned state. If no Internet-Draft is published within the 18 months, or one of them expires after the 18 months, IANA moves the option to the Unassigned state, and it may then be assigned to any new publicly defined options.

Sites presently using site-specific option codes within the reclassified range should take steps to renumber those options to values within the remaining range. If a site needs more than 31 site-specific options, the site must switch to using suboptions, as has been done for other options such as the Relay Agent Information Option of RFC 3046.
sections.plainLanguage: The codes move through four states. They start as unavailable, so nobody new can have them. A vendor who already uses a code has six months to say so, which moves it to tentatively assigned, and 18 months to write a draft describing it, which moves it to assigned. Anything unclaimed after six months, or whose draft is not finished after 18 months, goes back to being free for anyone to use.

sections.title: What IANA Is Asked to Do
sections.content:
IANA is requested to expand the publicly defined DHCPv4 options space from 1 to 127 to 1 to 223. The new options, 128 to 223, are to be listed as Unavailable and must not be assigned to any publicly defined options.

IANA is further requested to receive notices from vendors that have been using one or more of the options in the 128 to 223 range, saying that they are using the option and are willing to document that usage, and to list these options as Tentatively Assigned.

Third, IANA is asked to change the listing of any options listed as Unavailable to Available six months from the publication date of the memo, after which these options may be assigned in accordance with RFC 2939.

Fourth, IANA is asked to change the listing of any options listed as Tentatively-Assigned to Unavailable 18 months from the publication date and periodically thereafter, as long as an option is listed as Tentatively-Assigned, if no un-expired Internet-Draft exists documenting the usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo spells out the four registry actions: grow the public range, list the new codes as unavailable, accept the claims from vendors, and move anything unclaimed or undocumented back to being free.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document in and by itself provides no security, nor does it impact the existing DHCP security as described in RFC 2131.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo changes no protocol behaviour, so it makes no difference to the security of DHCP itself.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS OF MAKING ROOM

items.title: 16-bit options in 126 and 127
items.text: Proposed by Ralph Droms in late 1996. It penalised the first option assigned to the new space, because 16-bit option support had to be implemented. These codes were reclaimed.

items.title: A new magic cookie
items.text: Penalised the first option in the new space, could affect existing clients that do not check the cookie, needed support for both message formats, and needed multiple DHCPDISCOVER messages.

items.title: Reclassifying part of the site range
items.text: Chosen, because the impact is minimal: only sites already using options in the reclassified range need to renumber.

items.label: Not yet assignable
items.desc: Where the reclassified options start. They must not be assigned to any publicly defined option.

items.label: Claimed by a vendor
items.desc: The vendor has told IANA and the working group that it uses the code and is willing to document it.

items.label: Free
items.desc: The option may now be assigned to any new publicly defined option in accordance with RFC 2939.

items.label: Published
items.desc: The usage has been published as an RFC, so IANA moves the option to this state.
